Introduction - April 2012 











##### **The risks to the base metals sector are rising** 

Thomson Reuters GFMS’ base metal index stands at just below 290 in mid April, down 10.3% from the high for the year of 322.58 recorded on February 8.  However, the index remains comfortably above the level of 277 seen at the start of the year and the 2011 fourth quarter low of 268.6.  In some respects, the decline in prices can be viewed as quite modest given the deterioration in

underlying conditions. 

The base metals sector appears to have priced in the worst of the Eurozone debt crisis.  However, the recent switch of attention to the problems in Spain provides a perhaps unwelcome reminder that the debt issue is by no means restricted to some of the more peripheral economies within the Eurozone. 

In last month’s report we noted that “caution on Chinese growth brings the (base metal) rally to a halt”.  Since then, we have had further confirmation of the slowdown in the rate of Chinese growth with the GDP, industrial production and fixed asset investment data.  However, this should not have come as a surprise to the base metal markets as many of the more industry specific data has been bearish for some time, and importantly there is little indication of an immediate rebound in underlying activity. 

###### **A supply response may, however, be slow to emerge** 

In the previous issue of the _Base Metals One Year Forecast_ , we considered the full year mine production numbers for 2011.  With the exception of copper and tin, mine output registered strong gains.  Although prices have fallen from their first quarter highs, they generally remain above the marginal costs of production and, consequently, Thomson Reuters GFMS is not expecting an immediate supply response.  Even for aluminium, where the cost pressures are the most extreme, production is now back on an upward trend after the cutbacks made in September last year (mainly in China).  The problem for the aluminium industry is that new lower cost smelters are being ramped up in the western part of the country, which is offsetting the closure of small-scale high-cost plants in the east of China. 

A similar situation prevails in the nickel industry where there is a general move down the cost curve by the nickel pig iron (NPI) producers as companies integrate more with the stainless steel sector.  Previously, it was estimated that the NPI suppliers typically had production costs in the region $18,000-19,000/tonne.  Despite the sharp decline in nickel prices we have not seen a significant cutback from this source.  The most likely factor to trigger lower Chinese nickel pig iron output is the impending ban on nickel ore exports from Indonesia. 

Autos and construction are two key sectors in terms of Chinese base metals demand.  For the former, auto production registered a dramatic slowdown in growth last year and figures for the first two months of this year show a 4.9% year-on-year decline to 2.95 million units.  In addition, the data relating to the construction sector is mixed.  New residential dwellings (based on floor space) was 14% down up to February at 70 million square metres; however floor space still under construction was 36% higher.  The production of other metal-intensive goods such as electrical generation equipment, air conditioners and washing machines all registered year-on-year declines. 

As we have discussed in our earlier reports, cost considerations

for the other base metals – copper, lead, tin and zinc – are not an issue at the moment. For copper and tin, prices are well in excess of the marginal costs of production, with elevated prices supported by the tight fundamentals. Thomson Reuters GFMS has just released its _Copper Survey 2012_ . Our analysis suggests that the marginal cost for copper is $4,410/tonne. For lead and zinc, any supply response will be delayed by the high level of byproduct prices. In addition to economic growth rates easing in China, Indian expansion is also slowing.  Industrial production grew 4.1% year-on-year in February, while growth in January was revised down to just 1.1%.  The largest decline was from the metals-intensive capital goods sector, reflecting poor confidence from Indian businesses.  High inflation and the large government deficit are adding to the country’s woes. 

Most of the recent US economic data remains positive for the base metals sector.  Although the US auto sales figures for March at 14.4 million units on a seasonally adjusted annualised rate (SAAR) basis were down from the extraordinarily high February figure, the overall first quarter level of 14.5 million units was the highest seen since 2008. Sales are driven by pent-up demand, improved confidence in the economy, demand for fuel-efficient vehicles, and easing credit conditions. 

The broader measure of US manufacturing activity provided by the ISM index continues to trend higher, rising from 52.4 in February to 53.4 in March.  Of slight concern for base metal demand is the weakness in export orders, highlighting that the US recovery will inevitably be held back somewhat by the much weaker economic environment in the Eurozone.

**A1** Aluminium - April 2012 ###### **Market background** After having rallied to just over $2,300/tonne on February 28th, following the sharp sell-off over the fourth quarter, aluminium prices have, on an official basis, been trending downwards. Although prices did rebound somewhat in early March, the recovery was short-lived. Aluminium has been no exception to the wider problems p

revailing in the global economy. Consequently, the latest bout of news flows has driven prices in mid-April to their lowest levels since the start of the year. The cash quote is currently trading at just above $2,000/tonne, however down just 1% on the start of the year. The metal’s fundamentals have not exactly been too inspiring either. Stocks on the LME have comfortably risen above 5 million tonnes; however are down marginally on the alltime high of 5.12 tonnes recorded on February 24th. As have highlighted in previous editions of this report, a large proportion of this material is tied up in warehousing deals, due to attractive forward spreads and low interest rates, and as a result is not available to the market. The lack of physical availability from LME warehouses together with lower LME aluminium prices, which has increased buying among consumers, has in turn seen premiums on the spot market escalate. The Midwest premium in the United States, for example, recently hit an 11-month high. A similar trend is also evident in Europe, with the duty-paid premium now in a range of $200-210/ tonne, compared with $145-180/tonne at the start of the year. In Japan, buyers have agreed to pay second-quarter premiums of between $115 and $127/tonne, up from $112/ tonne in the first quarter. ###### **Latest stock data point to improving demand** Producer stocks were down in February, with the latest data by the International Aluminium Institute (IAI) suggesting they totalled 1.426 million tonnes, down 4.5% on the previous month. Going forward, End-use data confirm that demand growth in the country has been easing in recent times. In January, Alcoa announced it would permanently shut the smelter by mid-year, due to rising raw material costs and falling aluminium prices. Despite further potential capacity curtailments, the company maintains a positive view of aluminium demand. ###### **Market outlook** Thomson Reuters GFMS see no reason to change their supply-demand balance and price projections for 2012. Demand conditions are generally expected to remain weak over the remaining part of the first half of the year. However, a second half recovery should see an overall increase of 3.2% in consumption this year. Together with limited production growth, we are forecasting the market to shift to a small deficit of 130,000 tonnes in 2012. This does not necessarily imply that the 2012 average price will be above last year’s average of $2,400/tonne, instead we believe that in line with the large LME inventory overhang (despite a large proportion of this material tied up in financing deals) prices will average $2,344/tonne, down 2.2%. This figure remains unchanged from our last report, as we correctly predicted a first quarter average of around $2,180/tonne. **Scenario B** is largely predicated on a faster than expected recovery in demand, as the debt crisis is resolved, and production growth in China eases. Under this scenario, we are expecting prices to average $2,507/tonne. By comparison, **Scenario C** anticipates yet another year of substantial surplus in the aluminium market, as Chinese producers bring on new smelting capacity. Cumulative first quarter sales rose 11.8% year-on-year and stood at 14.4 million units in March (on a seasonally adjusted annualised basis). Whilst down on the 15.1 million unit pace seen in the prior month, this represented a notable recovery from the 13.1 million and 11.7 million unit levels seen in March 2011 and March 2010 respectively. In contrast, the latest available data from Battery Council International showed replacement battery shipments falling 11.2% month-on-month and 10.8% year-on-year in January to 8.295 million units. hin the country tightens** Positively for the market, whilst the milder winter has dampened battery demand within the United States, it has also served to restrict the supply of spent batteries to secondary smelters, which use this scrap material as feed to produce refined metal. Production from secondary sources accounted for 91.0% of refined lead production in the United States last year according to ILZSG statistics. Furthermore, supply of higher grade material has also tightened following the suspension of Doe Run’s primary smelter in Herculaneum, Missouri, in late March after a fire damaged some equipment. The company has declared force majeure on lead shipments from the 130,000 tonne per year smelter, which is not expected to restart until May. Most notably the increase will come from laterites, as opposed to sulphide projects, for which there are limited new discoveries and of those that exist, their ore bodies have already been fully explored. 

The most obvious source of additional output will be from the next generation of high pressure acid leach (HPAL) projects.  These are mainly of 50,000 tonne plus capacity and once online have the potential to move the market into a substantial surplus.  However, as their history highlights, these are technically complex and operationally demanding. They involve huge capital costs and geographically, the next bout of projects are based in regions with limited infrastructure and high political risk, most notably in South East Asia and Africa.  Furthermore, once on stream, the technology has a tendency to be plagued by “teething” problems, which is why we question the length of time it will take for these projects to ramp-up to full capacity.  A clear example of this is Minara Resources’ Murrin Murrin mine, which has a design capacity of around 40,000 tonnes, but has never reached this level since coming online in the late 1990s.  However, one thing that must be remembered is that the first generation of PAL projects were commissioned by
